'''''Dipogon lignosus''''', the '''okie bean''', '''Cape sweet-pea''', '''dolichos pea''' or '''mile-a-minute vine''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[legume]] family, [[Fabaceae]]. It is the only species classified in the monotypic genus '''''Dipogon'''''<ref>[http://www.tropicos.org/Name/40033099 Tropicos, ''Dipogon'' Liebm.]</ref>  which belongs to the subfamily [[Faboideae]].<ref>Liebmann, Frederik Michael. 1854.  Annales des Sciences Naturelles; Botanique, série 4, vol 2: 374</ref>

==Description==
''Dipogon lignosus'' is climbing woody, herbaceous perennial which becomes woody towards the base. The soft green stems climb over nearby structures, shrubs or trees, and can grow up to 2{{nbsp}}m tall, extending a long way horizontally if possible. Its leaves are dark to medium green above, paler below and are composed of three diamond shaped leaflets which have a wide set base before tapering to a fine point. Each leaflet has its own stalk. The flowers are typical for the pea family and are pink, mauve, magenta and purple in colour, growing on the tips of new growth stems in short, dense [[raceme]]s with long peduncles. Flowering occurs throughout spring and summer, i.e. August to January in its native [[South Africa]]. The pods are flat and sickle-shaped, each containing four to six seeds, and are formed soon after flowering. In warmer climates this is an evergreen, but it may develop a deciduous habit in areas where are subject to frosts.<ref name = plantz>{{cite web | url = https://www.plantzafrica.com/plantcd/dipogonlignosus.htm | title = Dipogon lignosus (L.) Verdc. | accessdate = 13 March 2017 | publisher = www.plantzafrica.com. | author1 = Rebecca Wengrowe | author2 = Alice Notten | year = 2012}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Dipogon lignosus'' has a native range that covers the [[Western Cape]] and [[Eastern Cape]] in South Africa where it prefers milder areas where it is not subjected to frost.<ref name = plantz/> It is an invasive weed in Australia<ref name = eurobodalla>{{cite web | url = http://www.esc.nsw.gov.au/living-in/about/our-natural-environment/introduced-plants-and-animals/weeds/weed-profiles/dolichos-pea-dipogon-lignosus | title = Dolichos pea (''Dipogon lignosus'') | accessdate = 13 March 2017 | publisher = Eurobodalla Shire Council | archive-date = 14 March 2017 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170314063504/http://www.esc.nsw.gov.au/living-in/about/our-natural-environment/introduced-plants-and-animals/weeds/weed-profiles/dolichos-pea-dipogon-lignosus | url-status = dead }}</ref> and New Zealand<ref name = "mile-a-minute">{{cite web | url = http://www.biosecurity.govt.nz/pests/mile-a-minute | title = Mile-a-minute ''Dipogon lignosus'' | accessdate = 13 March 2017 | publisher = [[Ministry for Primary Industries (New Zealand)|Ministry for Primary Industries]] | archive-date = 14 March 2017 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170314152445/http://www.biosecurity.govt.nz/pests/mile-a-minute | url-status = dead }}</ref>  and in some areas control of ''D. lignosus'' can be mandated.<ref name = SA>{{cite web | url = http://www.pir.sa.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0011/234587/dolichos_pea.pdf | title = dolichos pea | accessdate = 13 March 2017 | publisher = [[Government of South Australia]] | archive-date = 3 April 2016 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160403094508/http://pir.sa.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0011/234587/dolichos_pea.pdf | url-status = dead }}</ref>

==Habitat and biology==
In South Africa ''Dipogon lignosus'' has a natural habitat of forest margins and stream banks, where it climbs over other shrubs and trees.<ref name = plantz/> This habitat preference is replicated in Australia but it is usually found close to human habitation.<ref name = eurobodalla/> It prefers to grow in moderately shady sites where there is dense vegetation to provide support for its twining stems.<ref name = SA/>

The seeds are explosively thrown out of the ripe pods landing some distance from the parent plant and they are able to remain dormant in the soil for some years when conditions are unfavourable for germination. Germination is stimulated by disturbance such as fire, rain or seasonal changes. As a [[legume]] ''D. lignosus'' has symbiotic nitrogen fixing bacteria  which live on nodules on the roots and these enhance soil fertility The bacteria are afforded nutrients and shelter by the planta and the bacteria provide their host with usable nitrogen collected from minerals in the soil.<ref name = plantz/> It is tolerant of salt laden winds.<ref name = SA/>

==Horticulture==
''Dipogon lignosus'' has been widely cultivated outside of South Africa from as far back as the early nineteenth century. Areas where it has been used in horticulture include Europe, [[Madeira]], [[Azores]], [[Sri Lanka]], Australia, [[California]] and temperate regions of South America.<ref name = plantz/>

==Invasion==
''Dipogon lignosus'' is regarded as highly invasive in Australia especially in riverside and coastal vegetation, [[heathland]], dry [[sclerophyll]] forest, warm temperate rainforest and grassland. It is an effective invader as the seed is explosively ejected from pods over distances of several metres or the seeds may be spread further in dumped garden refuse or contaminated soil and it is also dispersed by birds or water for distances that may exceed 1 km.  Rhizomes can also be transported to spread the plant.<ref name = SA/>

Control of ''D. lignosus'' in native Australian vegetation can be very labour-intensive and the best control strategy is to minimise disturbance by removing the smaller, scattered plants initially and then targeting the larger infestations starting at their outer margins. The small seedlings may be sprayed with a suitable herbicide where appropriate. For larger plants, the climbing stems should be cut down to the roots with the remnant stumps then being excavated or immediately treated with herbicide.<ref name = SA/>

==Taxonomy and nomenclature==
The [[Specific name (botany)|specific name]] ''lignosus'' means woody in [[Latin]], referring to the woody stems base at the base of the plant. ''Dipogon'' is derived from  the [[Greek language|Greek]] ''di'', meaning two, and ''pogon'' meaning beard, referring to the [[Style (botany)|style]] which has a thick beard on its upper side near its tip.<ref name = plantz/>

Originally it was placed in the genus ''[[Dolichos (plant)|Dolichos]]'', hence the Australian vernacular name of dolichos pea, and [[Carl Linnaeus]] named the spcesies as ''Dolichos lignosus''. [[Bernard Verdcourt]] moved it into the monotypic genus ''Dipogon'' in 1968 when he was revising the genus ''Dolichos'', using the name ''Dipogon'' which had been used by [[Frederik Liebmann|Liebmann]] in 1854 and  as it was an already established synonym for ''Dolichos lignosus''.<ref name = plantz/>
